#9841. The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository. If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works. Let’s go!

3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY. There are also many representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.

TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.

The same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.

A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.

Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task.

Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.

LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide.

Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:

Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.

TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.

First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.

The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.

O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.

Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.

We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.

In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.

Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.

We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.

Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.

If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.

A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.

To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub:

Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:

We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.

The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline. See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository.

For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:

This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here. The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later.

The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.

We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later.

If you set --push-to, the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity. A compact script is also available in the same repository.

If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have, feel free to use the following set of commands.

The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different.

If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands:

Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso

We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again.

We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training.

Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object

The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train (ss or shape), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning.

We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model(). This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface.

We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point (fp32) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 (bf16) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored.

It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3, Flux 2, and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching.

We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen.

The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands.

We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images.

We then follow these steps within the training loop:

The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches.

For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps.

We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours.

The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry.

Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects.

The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans.

We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set:

In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects.

For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space.

Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs, and evaluated the outputs on held-out objects.

The main lesson is to select a training target that agrees with the problem and the data that you have. For this experiment, we fine-tuned the structure and shape stages and froze the texture stage.

Next, we can examine if the same choices help other 3D generation models, such as Pixal3D and UniLat3D.

Gaussian-splat and world-generation models, such as HunyuanWorld 2.0 and NVIDIA Lyra 2.0, are also possible next steps. Their representations and training pipelines can need different methods.

Thank you for following along, and see you in the next one! 👋🤗

#9840. How I Built an On-Device Trading Card Scanner With Apple Vision

Solo iOS and Flutter developer. I build small iPhone apps (sourdough planning, trading card scanning, pet records, Screen Time blockers) and write a

Solo iOS and Flutter developer. I build small iPhone apps (sourdough planning, trading card scanning, pet records, Screen Time blockers) and write a

Solo iOS and Flutter developer. I build small iPhone apps (sourdough planning, trading card scanning, pet records, Screen Time blockers) and write a

How the scanner in Foilcase works out which printing of a trading card it is looking at: Vision feature prints for the artwork, text recognition for the collector number, and a strict rule for when to ask instead of guessing. Plus the storage underneath it: an append-only ledger and one daily price file for everyone. Foilcase is my iPhone app for scanning and pricing cards from five trading card games (App Store); the user-facing write-up covers what it does.

Before release I built a harness on a Mac that calls the same Vision APIs as the app: 9,903 cards indexed, 400 queries, half drawn on purpose from collector numbers that more than one print shares. Each query was a synthetic degradation of an official card image (perspective, blur, glare, colour cast, JPEG).

Artwork, top-1 when given the correct number

The last row changed the design. Even with the right collector number, artwork matching picks the right print 89.5% of the time, because alternate arts and higher-rarity parallels often share one number and one illustration. No embedding separates two prints of one picture, so the app asks which print, as it asks whether a card is foil. And since five candidates nearly always include the right card, the five-card sheet is the main flow, not an error state.

The embedding is VNGenerateImageFeaturePrintRequest, revision 2: 768 floats, about 9 ms an image. One option matters more than it looks:

The default, .centerCrop, cuts the top and bottom off a tall card: 82.4% against 93.2% for .scaleFill on the same 1,295-card index. The probe exists because feature prints fail in the Simulator ("Failed to create espresso context"). The app checks once and falls back to the collector number alone, as it would on any device without a usable neural engine.

The obvious next step is a distance threshold. Measured, it says almost nothing: median distance was 0.450 when the top match was right and 0.420 when it was wrong. But distance does tell whether there is a card at all: photographed cards sat at a median of 0.459, a phone pointed at a laptop at 0.966. I found that out when the scanner, with no ceiling, turned a browser window into twenty-six confident entries. The ceiling is now 0.80, which keeps 99% of photographed cards and rejects 89% of everything else.

The number is unambiguous whenever it is legible, so most of the work went into legibility.

Drop soft frames. Between a handheld frame and a sharp one, the artwork gained 5.6 points and the collector number 46 (32.8% read against 78.5%). The gate is the variance of the Laplacian on a greyscale buffer of the rectified card. My first version chained Core Image filters, a Laplacian then a multiply blend, and returned negative variances: blend modes clamp and premultiply, they are not arithmetic.

Don't ask Vision to find the card. On iOS, VNDetectDocumentSegmentationRequest returned the card's text box at 0.96 confidence, and VNDetectRectanglesRequest found artwork panels, never the border. So the scanner draws a card-shaped guide, tries three crops around it and keeps whichever embeds closest to the index.

Read in passes, at full size. Downscaling crops is how my first benchmark reported an OCR accuracy of zero. VNRecognizeTextRequest runs over the whole card, then the top and bottom 22% enlarged 2.5 times, then three corners at 4 times if nothing turned up:

The recognizer swaps look-alikes (S and 5, O and 0, B and 8), so readings are folded before comparing. That tolerance is what kept producing wrong additions. The fix was two keys: a loose one, padding removed, for finding candidates, and a literal one, padding and variant marks kept, for adding without asking. "45/195" fits a catalog "045/195", but it is also what "145/195" looks like with its first digit lost.

Add without asking only when the artwork's first choice (or a card it can't tell apart from it) and a reading that spells that card's number literally name the same card, and nothing the artwork can't rule out shares that number. Everything else is the sheet. Trimmed from ScanPipeline.decide:

A different card sharing the number stops blocking only if the artwork puts it at least 15% farther away. unpadded lets an old card printed "18/130" match a catalog "018/130", but only when it lands on the artwork's own first pick.

The rule took three rounds of adversarial review to reach, each reported bug reproduced against the real catalogs. The first confirmed 33 defects; the second found 12 new ones, 11 introduced by the fixes. As my commit message put it, a comparison built to find candidates was also allowed to add one. Adding on artwork margin alone went too: a card missing from the index still has a nearest neighbour that can be clearly ahead and wrong.

Before a silent add, a second text request also counts Han, kana and hangul characters, because artwork and number are identical across languages and each catalog holds one. English cards read 0 to 3, Japanese ones 37 to 188; the cut-off is 8.

Then I measured on 529 real photographs of cards, labelled against the catalog, with all five games installed (62,331 cards in one index) and the app's recognition code running on a Mac. Every silent add was checked by eye:

The gains came from the photos: a picked photo now skips the quality gates, since no better frame is coming; the number is read from the loosest crop when the tightest cut it off; and each crop is also embedded slightly blurred, because a holo's sparkle pulled matches away from the flat scans in the index (right card first: 377 to 397). The live camera path is still unmeasured; for that, the app keeps an on-device calibration log of each attempt and the card the user actually picked.

Each game's index downloads separately, quantised to int8 with one scale per pack. On queries perturbed to the distance a handheld photo sits at, int8 and float16 returned the same card 99.8% of the time, for half the bytes. There's no approximate nearest-neighbour library: in the Mac harness, a brute-force scan of the largest index, 26,978 vectors, takes 1.6 ms widened to Float, but holds 83 MB. So the app memory-maps the int8 bytes and converts 512 rows at a time with vDSP_vflt8 and vDSP_distancesq: 5.6 ms, nothing resident. The scan runs only on a steady frame, so four milliseconds is invisible and 83 MB isn't. A pack from a different Vision revision is refused; its distances live in another space.

The index is built on a Mac and lags the catalog, so a clearly read number naming a card the artwork never offered goes to the top of the sheet, asked about and never added.

The collection is an append-only ledger table plus an items table derived from it in the same transaction. Removal is a tombstone; rebuild() replays the log. Replay needs an order every device agrees on, and the middle term of the sort key is a bug fix: the scanner adds a card and sets its finish within one millisecond, and a random event id sometimes sorted the edit first.

It paid off in October. The upstream catalog renamed sets, card ids include the set name, and 1,323 cards in one game got new ids overnight, 222 more across the others. Copies saved under old ids dropped off the collection screen. The fix is an alias table read in memory; the log stays as written.

Prices are one binary file per game, the same bytes for every user, so a request says nothing about what anyone owns. Names are content-addressed and the manifest is written last, so a client never sees half an update. Prices are integer cents, with a sentinel so a $0.00 promo isn't an unpriced card. Each carries the day it was captured, and past PriceProvenance.staleAfterDays (7) the portfolio headline says "These prices are 2 weeks old" instead of presenting an old total as current.

What the app does for the people who use it: Scan trading cards and see what they're worth with Foilcase.

Mostly not from the image: in my pre-release harness, artwork matching picked the right print 89.5% of the time even when given the correct collector number. Foilcase reads the number with Vision text recognition and, when other prints share it, shows the candidates and asks.

For retrieval, yes, with no model to ship: the right card was in the top five 99.8% of the time on sharp synthetic frames of a 9,903-card index. Use .scaleFill, and test on a device, because it doesn't run in the Simulator.

Not at tens of thousands of vectors. A brute-force Accelerate scan over 26,978 feature prints took 1.6 ms on a Mac in Float, or 5.6 ms as memory-mapped int8, which avoids holding 83 MB in memory.

Not between similar images: median distance was 0.450 for correct matches and 0.420 for wrong ones. It does separate cards (0.459) from non-cards (0.966), so Foilcase uses it only as a 0.80 ceiling.

Lower minimumTextHeight, turn off language correction, never downscale the crop, and add passes over enlarged strips and corners. Rejecting blurry frames first matters most: it took collector-number accuracy from 32.8% to 78.5% in my harness.

Nothing is overwritten, so a mis-tap or a bug can't destroy data: removal is a tombstone and the item table is rebuilt from the log. Changed upstream ids resolve through an alias table at read time, without touching user data.

#9839. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

#9838. The Psychology of Luxury Marketing: Why We Pay More for Less

Hi, I'm Yukti Sachan, a writer and content creator from India with an interest in storytelling, books, marketing, and formula 1

Hi, I'm Yukti Sachan, a writer and content creator from India with an interest in storytelling, books, marketing, and formula 1

Hi, I'm Yukti Sachan, a writer and content creator from India with an interest in storytelling, books, marketing, and formula 1

Have you ever looked at a piece of bent metal and thought, “Why does this cost as much as a decent used car?”

Recently, I stumbled across a Ferrari metal collar online. It cost $2,500. It looked like someone picked up a sheet of basic aluminum, bent it aggressively, painted it Rosso Corsa red, and said, “Yep, that’ll be two grand and a half, please.”

It made me genuinely sit down and ask: Why the fuck would anyone pay that?

Well, welcome to a niche little world called luxury marketing, which apparently means we add a ridiculous price tag to ordinary items and watch everyone scramble to buy them.

Luxury marketing has three main pillars that conveniently work together to gaslight you into thinking that a tiny bottle of perfume = a down payment for a prime city apartment is a completely reasonable thing to pay for.

The three main pillars of luxury marketing are: I know those sound like really scary terms, but trust me, I’m going to hold your hand and explain how they collectively gaslight you.

(Disclaimer: I’m not a marketing person. All of this has come from research papers and articles I’ve read, plus whatever marginal bits I actually understood from them. 😭)

When you think something you want is about to sell out, you’re more likely to impulsively buy it, even if you haven’t stopped to think about the pros and cons yet. You see something you like, notice that there is very little stock left, and suddenly you’re buying it without thinking about whether you actually need it or not.

That’s essentially what the illusion of scarcity is: less availability, more wanting, quicker decisions, more impulsive buying, more urgency, and ultimately, more sales.

The illusion of scarcity refers to the tactic of creating a perception that a product or service is in limited supply when, in reality, it might not be.

It plays on the psychological principle that people are more likely to desire something they believe is running out or hard to obtain.

It compels people to take action when they believe they might miss out on something valuable or desirable.

The illusion of scarcity uses this fear to make customers more likely to buy to avoid the regret of missing out.

People are more motivated by the prospect of avoiding loss rather than gaining something.

The illusion of scarcity creates a sense of potential loss. Consumers fear losing the opportunity to purchase the product or service. This fear of loss motivates consumers more than the desire to gain, pushing them to act quickly.

When a consumer sees that a product is in limited stock or others are purchasing it quickly, they are more likely to believe the product is valuable and worth buying. The perception is reinforced by the idea that if others are scrambling to buy it, it must be worth having.

(Shameless advertisement: I talk more about this in my July edition, where I talked about how Red Bull used this tactic in the trash can myth. For more info, click here — July Edition.)

In luxury marketing, people aren’t just buying the product; they are buying the perceived social status that the said product provides them with.

In emerging markets (such as the BRIC nations, i.e., Brazil, Russia, India, and China), it was observed that logo-flashy or more easily recognised luxury goods are more widely sought after by people, as they felt the need to separate themselves from the masses and perceive a higher social status, like Look at me, I am richer as compared to you, which is why I am higher on the social ladder as compared to you and make themselves stand out.

Meanwhile, mature markets (such as the United States, Italy, and France) were observed to be moving towards more subtle, less flashy luxury items which aren’t very easily recognisable by someone who doesn’t know about it because they tend to do it for (so-called) internalised-luxury consumption. The term refers to the perception of purchasing luxury goods for themselves or to express themselves better and to integrate themselves into a certain social group.

Mature market, in the above context, refers to markets that have reached a certain equilibrium and are characterised by modest growth.

An emerging market, in the above context, refers to markets that have a chronic shortage of resources and are characterised by inadequate infrastructure but also yield impressive economic growth.

So, in mature markets, people are moving towards a more subtle display of luxury, such as minimalistic or no logos, or a higher emphasis on the craftsmanship of the product. While emerging markets move more towards flashy, easily recognisable logos or/and patterns.

Yet in general, both aren’t buying the product for the utilitarian purpose of the product, but rather are purchasing the product or service to display a certain social status and separate themselves from the masses, such as: I am different from you; I have a higher perceived social status than you; and I’m richer than you, and I have a certain expensiveness that you lack and am living a certain level of luxurious lifestyle that you cannot attain.

Luxury marketing emphasizes the item's perceived social status. And consumers invest in it as they associate a certain sense of self-importance and a separation from the masses and their supposed (*air quotes*) superior social status with the ownership of the product, and therefore are willing to invest more in products that are marketed as a luxury, with the illusion of scarcity, than what might be the actual justified cost of the product solely based on utility if it wasn’t marketed as a luxury good or service.

Heritage is a crucial part of a luxury brand, as it needs to have a modern aspect for the current society yet, at the same time, have a certain historical aspect to it.

It adds an association of depth, authenticity, and credibility to the brand's perceived value and can result in increased brand loyalty and a willingness to accept higher prices.

It marks within itself the strategic cultivation of the brand’s origins, traditions, and values over time. As Heritage builds on permanence, prestige, and authenticity, it gives luxury consumers a narrative and a mythology to associate themselves with, linking back to how they view their perceived social status increasing with consumption of luxury brands’ goods and/or services.

raise_for_status() turns a rejected key or a bounced request into an exception, which send_email catches and logs. Without it, a 401 from the provider would look like a success, and you'd find out from users who never got their email.

#9835. Postgres not using your index? It's counting pages, not rows

Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at hackernoon.com

Slow Postgres, part 1 of 8. The SQL and raw numbers for every test are on GitHub.

A Seq Scan reads each page once, in order. An index lookup walks the B-tree and then reads one heap page per TID.

You add an index on status, run EXPLAIN, and Postgres reads the whole table anyway. ANALYZE doesn't change the plan. Someone suggests SET enable_seqscan = off, the plan finally shows your index, and the query gets slower.

Usually the planner is right. It prices a plan by the 8 KB pages it has to read and by whether it reads them in order or jumps around between them, and once you count pages the same way, you can answer most "why is it ignoring my index" tickets yourself.

This series started as my notes from an open lesson on slow Postgres queries by balun.courses. The tests and numbers are my own.

One note before the numbers: the AlphaVPS link at the end is a referral link, so I may get a commission at no extra cost to you, and the netcup vouchers come from my own account.

A regular B-tree index keeps only keys, the values it is sorted by, and next to each key a TID: the row's address in the heap, which is the table's main storage.

A TID is a page number plus a slot on that page. You can see it as the hidden ctid column:

Row 1000 is slot 48 on page 7. An index lookup for 'chargeback' returns a list of addresses like these, and Postgres then visits each of those heap pages to fetch the row and check that your transaction can see it.

The second step is the one people forget. To fetch one row, Postgres has to read the whole 8 KB page it sits on.

The lab runs on PostgreSQL 17.11 in Docker with default settings. My numbers come from a 4-vCPU, 8 GB cloud VM, but any small VPS or a laptop will do.

136 rows fit on a page, so 30,000 rows take 221 pages. I picked 30,000 because ANALYZE samples 300 × default_statistics_target rows, which is 30,000 at the default. On this table it reads every row, so the statistics are exact and your plans should come out the same as mine.

Ask for the most common value and the index goes unused:

Cost has no unit you can convert to milliseconds. It only means something next to another plan's cost.

The value you filter on appears nowhere in that formula. Ask for 'chargeback' with the index paths switched off and the Seq Scan still costs 596. Only the index path's price moves with the value, so the planner is choosing between a fixed price and a sliding one.

For 'paid', every one of the 221 pages holds paid rows, so the index path would read the whole heap plus the index. Force it with enable_seqscan = off and you get a Bitmap Heap Scan at cost 872.

Selectivity is the share of rows that pass the filter. The usual rule of thumb goes: one row, use the index; 1%, usually; 20%, it depends; 70%, Seq Scan. Here is the same table counted by pages as well as by rows:

Share of rows and share of pages for each status in the 30,000-row table. failed is 0.9% of the rows but sits on 94% of the pages.

The rule of thumb says index failed, and Postgres agrees: Index Scan at cost 235 against 596. Run both with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), though, and the index path touches 209 buffers to the Seq Scan's 221, a saving of twelve page reads.

It still finished faster, 0.19 ms versus 0.93, because checking 270 rows is less CPU work than filtering 30,000. For 'chargeback', 30 rows on 30 pages, the index path needs 32 buffers instead of 221.

Two things decide how rows land on pages. Row width sets how many fit on one, and at 136 rows per page any value much more common than 1 in 136 ends up on nearly every page. Physical order is the other. I spread failed evenly on purpose. If your failed orders came from one bad deploy on one afternoon, they'd sit on a few neighbouring pages and the index would look great.

On 221 pages everything finishes in a couple of milliseconds, so for timings I built a bigger table: 5 million rows, 326 MB, about 120 rows per page.

A bucket column holds a random number from 0 to 999,999, so WHERE bucket < 10000 matches 1% of the rows. I loaded the same rows twice, once in random order and once sorted by bucket, and forced each plan with the enable_* settings at shares from 0.01% to 50%. shared_buffers was 2 GB, which kept the whole table in memory.

Median of 5 warm runs on 5 million rows, one process, JIT off. Dots mark the plan Postgres chose on its own. Grey dotted line: Seq Scan on the clustered copy.

For scattered rows Postgres picked a bitmap scan, which collects all the TIDs first and then reads each heap page once, in page order. Up to 10% of the rows it beat the Seq Scan, 98 ms to 124. At 25% it lost, 174 against 139, and the planner still chose it. A plain Index Scan, one heap visit per row, lost from 5% on.

By 10% the scattered matches sit on every single page, and the bitmap scan still won. It reads all 41,667 pages but checks only the 499,000 rows the bitmap points to, while the Seq Scan checks all 5 million. With the table in RAM a page read costs next to nothing, and the time goes into checking rows.

For clustered rows the index won at every share I tried, even 50%: 123 ms against 142.

RAM is the friendly case. For the cold runs I restarted Postgres and dropped the OS page cache before every run, so every page came off the VM's disk.

Same tables and queries read cold from disk, median of 5. Dots mark the plan Postgres chose. Grey dotted line: Seq Scan on the clustered copy.

The Seq Scan got about twice as slow, 250 to 350 ms at every share. The clustered index won everywhere again, 23 ms versus 263 at 5%.

The scattered bitmap scan took 748 ms at 0.5% of rows, to the Seq Scan's 349. At 1% it took 1.27 seconds against 255 ms, five times slower, and that's the plan Postgres picks.

The bitmap scan at 2% read more heap pages than at 1%, 37,939 versus 29,143, and still finished more than six times faster, 190 ms against 1,275. From 2% to 10% it beat the Seq Scan again.

The 2% run touched 91% of the pages, so it was close to one long sequential read. The 1% run touched 70%, with holes in between. My best guess is OS readahead, which prefetches reads that look sequential and gives up when they're full of gaps. I haven't confirmed it yet.

The planner has no way to see that difference. All it has is random_page_cost = 4, a single guess at how much a jump costs next to a sequential read, and it used the same guess for both runs.

A 200-row copy shows the other end of the scale, where the table is too small for any index to win.

Only 2 of the 200 rows match, but reading two pages and checking 200 rows costs just 2 + 2 + 0.5 = 4.50. Turn off enable_seqscan and the cheapest index plan costs 6.19, because its one index page alone is priced as a random read at random_page_cost = 4. If you check plans on a 200-row test fixture, this is the arithmetic you're looking at, and it tells you nothing about the same query on 30 million rows in production.

"We're on SSDs, set it to 1.1." Fair, and on this table that flips the plan to an Index Scan at cost 2.77. Both versions finish in 10 microseconds or less, so on a table this size it makes no difference.

The one place for enable_seqscan = off is a scratch session, where it shows you what the other plan would cost. It applies to every query in the session, so in app code it also overrides the plans that were right, like 596 against 872 for 'paid'.

If the queries you care about only ask for the rare values, say a failed-payments dashboard or a chargeback queue, index only those rows:

It holds 3,000 entries instead of 30,000 and takes 5 pages, where the full index takes 28. Paid orders, 90% of the inserts here, never touch it.

Postgres only uses it when it can prove your filter implies the index's WHERE, and a literal status = 'chargeback' does. With only the partial index in place, a prepared status = $1 under a generic plan falls back to a Seq Scan, because the planner can't prove anything about a value it hasn't seen. Generic plans get their own part later in the series.

Before adding an index, look at the column in pg_stats:

That's what the planner believes about status as of the last ANALYZE. If most of your queries filter on paid, at 0.9, they get a Seq Scan, and no extra index will change that.

A negative n_distinct means a fraction of the row count. On tables bigger than the 30,000-row sample these numbers are estimates; you can raise the sample with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS.

The same view has a correlation column, the planner's idea of physical order. On my 5-million-row tables it was 0.01 for the scattered copy and 1 for the clustered one, and that difference in physical order is what separates the scattered and clustered lines in both charts.

Before CREATE INDEX, run the pg_stats query, relpages and the rows-versus-pages count on your own table. If the value you care about sits on most of the pages and the table doesn't stay in memory, the index won't save you reads.

All the numbers above come from one 4-vCPU AMD EPYC cloud VM with 8 GB of RAM, so yours will differ. The SQL, the scripts, the raw output and the chart code are on GitHub. Run them on your own server, and if you get a different picture or think I got something wrong, open an issue or a PR.

My own projects run on netcup (VPS from €2.21 a month) and AlphaVPS (VPS from €2.54 a month). If you need a box for this, either works.

For netcup I have a few €5 vouchers for new customers. Each one works once, so take one and leave the rest for the next person:

Paste it into the "Redeem voucher" field at the bottom of the netcup cart. If they're all gone, message me on LinkedIn and I'll send you a new one.

Good luck with your plans. Part 2 is next: how to read Postgres EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

#9834. Claude Merged 30,401 Changes in One Day. Git Couldn't Keep Up.

An agent gets a task - fix a flaky test. Before it reads a single line of code, it needs a working copy of the repository.

Under git, that meant waiting 7.1 minutes.

Multiply that wait by tens of thousands of agents a day and you get the problem Anthropic described in its engineering post on 13 October 2026. The code wasn't the slow part any more. Claude could write the fix in seconds; the plumbing built for human engineers (source control, builds, CI) couldn't hand it the repo fast enough.

So Anthropic threw out git for its main repository and built Scion.

The numbers tell the story better than I can. In January 2026, Anthropic merged roughly 1,000 code changes a day. By May it was about 2,500.

The team tried everything git offers to cope: shallow clones, sparse checkouts, promisor remotes, repository snapshots and several hundred git mirrors. Each one bought time. None of them bought enough, because the main-branch history was close to 100 GB and the compressed working copy was over 25 GB. CI alone ran around 25 million checkouts a day.

The mirrors eventually outgrew their disks. At that point you can split the monorepo (and lose speed) or rebuild source control. Anthropic picked the second option.

By September, Anthropic was merging more than 30,000 changes a day. The peak was 30,401 on 9 September. That's a 12x jump in four months, and most of it came from Claude.

That's the day git stopped being a tool and became a ceiling.

Scion looks more like Subversion than git, and Anthropic says so openly. Git assumes every client is a full copy of history that can work offline. Scion assumes the opposite: clients are always online, so the server does the heavy lifting.

Anthropic reports a cache hit rate above 99% at every tier. Almost nothing travels all the way to the servers.

The unit of history changes too. A git commit points to a full tree. A Scion changeset lists only the files that changed relative to its first parent, each with a content-addressed pointer to a compressed blob. The server works out trees, history and blame from those changesets when someone asks.

Branches are discouraged, except for main and release branches. Creating a changeset never touches a branch; moving one is a single compare-and-swap on one Spanner row. That's why 30,000 merges a day don't trip over each other.

Anthropic's post doesn't publish a single runbook, so this is the flow pieced together from what the team described. Follow one agent and one flaky test.

Step 1: Get a worktree in seconds. Claude asks scn for a working copy. It doesn't clone anything. The client names the root tree it wants and fetches only the objects it's missing, usually from the local daemon. Checkouts are sparse or virtual: a file lands on disk only when Claude opens it. A new agent worktree went from 7.1 minutes to 5.1 seconds, an 84x speedup.

Step 2: Ask the server questions instead of the disk. Where was this test last changed? Who touched this function? Under git, Claude would run git log or git blame over local history. Under Scion, history, blame and diffs are server queries exposed through an API. Many jobs never need a local repository at all; Anthropic says its automated bisect and revert pipelines wouldn't be practical at scale without this.

Step 3: Edit, and let status stay cheap. Claude changes two files. The client watches the filesystem rather than rescanning the whole tree, so checking status for an agent fell from 4.3 seconds to under 0.2.

Step 4: Commit straight to the server. A commit creates a changeset on the server, and it's visible everywhere at once. There's no push step and no packfile negotiation. An agent commit dropped from 18 seconds to 761 milliseconds.

Step 5: Open a change request in Antique. Antique is Anthropic's new code review tool, built alongside Scion. Reviewers check the intent of a change, not every line. Semantic approval rules can tell a comment-only edit apart from one that touches sensitive logic, so the review effort goes where the risk is. Review moved to Antique between May and June 2026; by August almost every merged change went through it.

Step 6: Merge without a global queue. Here's the part that surprised me. Anthropic dropped the old globally locked merge queue, because serialising 30,000 merges a day doesn't work. Changes merge concurrently. When two of them conflict, Claude repairs the conflict.

Step 7: Test after merge, before deploy. With no queue holding everything back, the safety net moves later. Post-merge and pre-deploy testing catches what pre-merge serialisation used to. If something breaks, the same cheap server-side history powers the automated bisect and revert.

Add it all up and the source-control overhead for one change request fell from 34 minutes to 3.7 minutes. Across roughly 22,000 change requests a day, that's a lot of machine time handed back.

There's a loop in this story I find hard to ignore. Claude created the load that broke git, and then Claude helped build the replacement.

Engineers set the architecture, the scaling targets and the invariants. Claude wrote much of the code; the source control and Antique directories received 12,257 changes between January and September. The team's original git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline was hand-written. They gave it to an early internal snapshot of Claude Mythos Preview and asked for a rewrite, with no further instructions. The new version used 20x less memory and ran 4x faster, and it kept the ordering rules the old one relied on.

The team also runs dedicated Claude instances that each watch one component's telemetry and logs (the daemon, the cache, Antique's merge flow). And the engineers' most common job, by their own account, was telling Claude "no"; for example, when it read the commit log instead of querying the review tool.

Scion isn't free. You lose offline work: no server, no source control. You also lose portability, because Scion only makes sense with Anthropic's own review, search and CI systems wired around it.

The results, as Anthropic reports them on its own workload:

The infrastructure footprint shrank about 200x compared with the git mirror fleet, and CI needed 25% less CPU. These aren't general benchmarks against git, and Anthropic is careful to say so.

You can't. Scion isn't open source, and Anthropic calls it "by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use."

What it does want is for git platforms to borrow the ideas: full server-side APIs, a better fetch protocol, and stronger sparse and shallow support for agent-sized workloads. It credits Google's Piper, Meta's Sapling and the Mononoke server (with its Bonsai data model) for many of the techniques.

If your team runs a handful of agents, git is fine. If you're heading toward thousands, look at where your agents spend their first seven minutes.

That's where Anthropic found 30,000 merges a day.

Sources: Anthropic Engineering, "Redesigning source control at Anthropic" (13 October 2026, updated 15 October); coverage by InfoQ, Simon Willison and Matthews Wong. All performance figures are company-reported.

#9833. Lessons from the November 2026 Microsoft 365 Outage: Designing Resilient OneDrive Transfers

Incident handling, Microsoft Graph throttling, resumable jobs, and the limits of cloud-to-cloud backup during a provider outage.

On November 12–13, 2026, a major Microsoft 365 service disruption exposed a familiar dependency: applications built on a cloud platform are only as reachable as the platform's identity, metadata, and file APIs.

Microsoft tracked incidents under MO1550821 (broader Microsoft 365 connectivity) and EX1550543 (Exchange Online). Public notices in Japan documented trouble accessing OneDrive alongside other Microsoft 365 applications; Hitotsubashi University's notice is one example.

The incident's reported infrastructure symptoms included unexpectedly unavailable servers and increased load. Those are incident reports, not proof that every Microsoft Graph endpoint failed or that any particular HTTP status code was widespread. What follows is an engineering playbook for the kinds of failures cloud-transfer systems may encounter during an outage.

A transfer failure can have several causes. Classify them before retrying:

These are general diagnostic examples, not a list of confirmed errors from the November incident. Microsoft documents their Graph error semantics separately.

For Microsoft 365 tenants, first correlate error spikes with Service Health and incident notices. Record timestamps, endpoint, tenant or account scope, sanitized error code, and request ID. Avoid logging OAuth tokens or file contents.

A naive retry loop can turn a bad incident into a worse one. Microsoft Graph's throttling guidance says to use Retry-After when supplied for 429 responses; otherwise, an exponential-backoff strategy is recommended.

A simplified policy—not a production-ready library—might look like this:

Real systems also need a retry budget, request deadlines, cancellation, respect for HTTP-date-form Retry-After, and careful distinction between retry-safe reads and operations that create side effects. Do not blindly replay a non-idempotent upload or finalize request. SDKs may already retry some Graph requests automatically, so check for double retry layers.

For repeated copies, avoid enumerating the entire drive every time. Where applicable, Microsoft Graph delta queries can track changes and reduce unnecessary polling. Your implementation must still handle deleted items, invalidated state, permissions, pagination, and eventual consistency.

If a one-way mirror replicates accidental deletion, you have two copies of the same mistake. A recovery design should ask whether the destination is separately accessible, whether it retains versions, whether deletion propagation is appropriate, and whether restores have been tested.

When OneDrive itself is inaccessible, a new API-driven copy may be impossible. The best outage-time option is usually a second copy that already exists in another provider or an offline store.

Not every team needs to build and maintain its own migration worker. RiceDrive is a cloud-to-cloud transfer product that lets users connect OneDrive to destinations such as Google Drive, Dropbox, MEGA, Box, pCloud, and selected object stores—without a manual local download/upload cycle.

The product supports 40+ cloud platforms and protocols. Available workflows include background tasks, transfer logs, filters, and scheduled transfers; the free tier includes 10GB of monthly transfer traffic.

A useful first workflow is OneDrive → a separate destination account, using one-way copy settings, a limited test folder, and post-transfer verification. Work or school accounts may require administrative approval, and file-sharing links and version history should not be assumed to migrate unchanged.

See the illustrated OneDrive backup and transfer guide for setup steps and provider considerations.

This is a product-level backup option, not a claim that RiceDrive internally implements every architectural pattern in the diagram above. Nor can RiceDrive read OneDrive files through an unavailable Microsoft API. Set up and validate the independent copy while both providers are operating normally.

Bottom line: Availability incidents will happen. The engineering goal is to make a temporary upstream failure visible, recoverable, and less disruptive to users—not to pretend that another API client can repair an unavailable source.

References: Microsoft Service Health · Hitotsubashi University outage report · Microsoft Graph throttling · Microsoft Graph delta queries.

Disclosure: This article is published by the RiceDrive team. RiceDrive is mentioned as one option for cloud-to-cloud transfers.

It searches for malware and compares code, theme, and plugin files with the records in the WordPress.org repository to verify their integrity and reports changes to you.

Akismet can help prevent spam from appearing on your site. Every day, it automatically checks every comment against a global database of spam to block malicious content. With Akismet, you also won’t have to worry about innocent comments being caught by the filter or false positives. You can simply tell Akismet about those and it will get better over time. It also checks your contact form submissions against its global spam database and weed out unnecessary fake information.

Contact Form 7 is a plug-in that allows you to create contact forms that make it easy for your users to send messages to your site. The plug-in was developed by Takayuki Miyoshi and lets you create multiple contact forms on the same site; it also integrates Akismet spam filtering and lets you customize the styling and fields that you want to use in the form. The plug-in provides CAPTCHA and Ajax submitting.

#9829. Jensen Huang's Nvidia Exit Is a Wake-Up Call for Startup Founders

This morning, November 12, 2026, Nvidia's board said Jensen Huang had resigned as President, CEO, and director, effective immediately. CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO. The board also named Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair, which tells you it had been a one-man show for 33 years.

The board's word is "resigned." Most headlines went with "ousted." Days earlier, CBS had reported the board was preparing to remove him. You decide which word fits.

Here's the short version. A New York Times report alleged multiple affairs, including one with a Singapore data-center executive whom U.S. officials reportedly suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence, at a firm that bought billions of dollars of Nvidia hardware. Another alleged affair was with a senior executive who reported directly to him. Huang had already admitted infidelity in a memo to employees on November 9. Then came national-security questions, demands from lawmakers, and a stock that fell roughly 10%, wiping out hundreds of billions in market value. After that, the end came quickly.

Set the morality aside for a minute, because the board didn't need to settle it. What I want founders to notice is the mechanics.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in a Denny's in 1993. He bet the company on GPUs, then on CUDA, then on AI, and grew it into a company worth more than $4 trillion. He is about as close to a founder-god as Silicon Valley has.

And he had no structural protection whatsoever.

Nvidia has a single class of stock: one share, one vote. Its board was made up of independent directors plus Jensen, and it could remove the CEO with or without cause by simple majority. Mark Zuckerberg can't be fired. Larry Page couldn't be fired. Jensen Huang, the man who made the AI age possible, could be shown the door in a week.

If that doesn't make every founder reading this check their charter, nothing will.

Founders don't usually lose control in one dramatic boardroom scene. They lose it gradually, through a series of small and individually reasonable decisions.

Act I: One share, one vote. For about sixty years the NYSE refused to list companies with dual-class shares. The idea was that voting power should track economic risk. Ford's 1956 IPO, where the family kept super-voting shares, was the famous exception. Media dynasties like the New York Times Company got a pass on the grounds of editorial independence.

Act II: Google changes the rules. In 2004, Larry Page and Sergey Brin took Google public with Class B shares carrying 10 votes each. The public bought it anyway. Facebook, LinkedIn, Snap, and Alibaba all followed. Hong Kong held out, lost Alibaba's $25 billion IPO to New York, and changed its rules in 2018. By 2021–22, about 47% of U.S. tech IPOs were dual-class.

Act III: the slow loss of your majority. This is the part nobody puts in the pitch deck. According to Carta's 2025–26 data, founders typically hold:

Capital intensity makes it worse. If your company works with atoms (chips, robots, biotech), you burn two to three times the cash of a SaaS company and sell more of the company at every round. Jensen is the hardware founder's cautionary tale: decades of capital-hungry growth, and nothing left to vote with when it counted.

The lesson: you don't lose control when the board votes. You lose it, one term sheet at a time, years before.

Every founder knows this story, and every founder assumes it couldn't happen to them.

In 1985, Steve Jobs was 30, a co-founder of Apple, and the person most responsible for its products and culture. He had no super-voting shares. The Macintosh launched to great reviews and disappointing sales. Jobs's "my way or the highway" style wore everyone out. John Sculley, the Pepsi executive Jobs had personally recruited with the famous "sugar water" pitch, moved to take away his operating authority.

Jobs tried to get Sculley removed instead. The plan leaked, the board backed Sculley, and Jobs, with no structural power at all, resigned and went off to start NeXT.

What followed was a twelve-year slide that brought Apple to within about 90 days of insolvency in 1997. The board, out of options, bought NeXT, mostly to get Jobs back. You know the rest: iMac, iPod, iPhone, and the most valuable company on Earth.

Dual-class advocates like to say that if Jobs had held super-voting stock, Apple would have skipped a lost decade.

Maybe. I'll give you the more uncomfortable version. The Jobs who got fired was probably not the Jobs who saved Apple. NeXT and Pixar humbled him and taught him things, and he came back a better CEO. Getting fired may have been the most valuable thing that ever happened to him, though it's hard to see it that way while it's happening.

Adam Neumann got the thing Jobs never had: 20 votes per share. The board couldn't fire him, investors couldn't overrule him, and he ran the company accordingly.

When the S-1 came out in August 2019, public investors saw $47 billion in lease obligations against $4 billion in committed revenue, plus governance that made Apple's 1985 board look like the Federalist Papers. The IPO collapsed and SoftBank had to fund a bailout. Neumann was out, and in 2023 the company filed for Chapter 11.

Here's the lesson I care about most. Super-voting stock does two things: it protects you from the market's panic, and it protects you from your own mistakes. The first is valuable. The second can kill the company. The same structure that would have saved 1985 Jobs from Sculley also saved Neumann from anyone who might have told him no.

So what should you actually do? Here is the playbook, roughly by stage. If you can, negotiate these terms when you have leverage, which means before you need the money.

The academics have a useful framework for this. Agency costs are the damage a founder does when nobody can stop them; that's WeWork. Principal costs are the damage investors do when they're in charge: panic, short-termism, and a buyback where an R&D budget should be. That's 1985 Apple.

Law professors Zohar Goshen and Richard Squire argue the right structure minimizes the sum of the two. A visionary founder in a 20-year bet like AI, VR, or rockets should get more insulation. A mature company with a founder who has drifted should get less.

The data supports this. Dual-class firms trade at a premium at IPO, because markets value the founder's vision. Around seven to ten years later, that premium tends to become a discount as the founder's economic stake shrinks while their votes don't.

So the goal isn't maximum control. It's control that fits where your company is in its life: enough insulation to make long-term bets, with a working mechanism for someone to say "stop" if you lose your way.

Jensen had plenty of the first and none of the second, which was fine for 33 years until this week. Neumann had too much of both. Jobs had none, and it took a lost decade to fix.

Here's what I expect over the next five years.

1. The Jensen effect on fundraising. Founders raising in 2027 will bring up Nvidia in every board-composition negotiation, and investors will bring up WeWork. Both are fair points.

2. Trust-based structures as the new middle ground. Anthropic's S-1 shows a new model. The founders hold a Class F share that gives them 50.1% of ordinary votes, while an independent Long-Term Benefit Trust with no economic stake elects a majority of the board. The founders control the shareholder vote, and the trust controls the board. OpenAI's foundation keeps exclusive power over its PBC's board even though Microsoft owns 27% of the equity. These are deliberate checks and balances in a company charter, and you'll see others copy them.

3. Sunsets become standard. Perpetual founder control is ending. Index providers, proxy advisors, and institutional investors all agree on that. Expect seven-to-ten-year sunsets to become the price of a dual-class IPO.

4. The jurisdiction wars continue. Delaware vs. Texas vs. Nevada. Your state of incorporation is now a strategic decision, not a box your lawyer checks.

5. Character as a governance mechanism. This is the uncomfortable one. As founders gain more structural protection, the remaining risks come from conduct: personal behavior, conflicts of interest, national security. Those risks don't care how many votes your shares carry.

My closing advice to every engineer-founder reading this:

Fight for control early, when it's cheap. Protect it with structure, not just goodwill. Give it an expiration date before someone else does. And above all, build a company and a character that a board would never want to fire.

Jensen Huang built one of the greatest companies in history and still lost it in a week. Your share structure can't fully protect you from yourself, so you'll have to manage that part on your own.

#9828. WordPress or Custom Code? How to Choose for Your Business Website

Choosing between WordPress and custom code is one of the first decisions for any new business website in India. Neither option is "better" in general. The right answer depends on what the site has to do, who will maintain it, and how much it will change over time.

WordPress works well when your site is mostly content: a home page, service pages, a blog, a contact form. Reasons teams choose it:

The trade-off is maintenance. Core, theme and plugin updates need regular attention, and every extra plugin adds some security and performance risk. A lean setup with few, well-supported plugins usually performs far better than a heavily stacked one.

Custom development (for example a Node, Laravel or Django application with a hand-built front end) is worth considering when:

The trade-off is cost and speed. Every feature is built and tested by your team or agency, and changes to content may need a developer unless a CMS is built in.

Also consider a hybrid: WordPress as a headless CMS with a custom front end, or a custom application sitting next to a WordPress blog on a subdomain. These can work, but they add moving parts, so use them only when there is a clear reason.

If you are weighing the two options for a real project, it helps to talk to a team that builds both and can explain trade-offs in plain language. You can learn about the services of a web development firm in India such as MGTech Labs, or browse practical guides on the MGTech Labs blog before you make a call.

Whichever route you choose, write down your requirements first, ask for a clear scope, and plan for maintenance from day one. A well-maintained simple site beats a neglected complex one every time.
