#9795. Postgres not using your index? It's counting pages, not rows

Full-stack Developer TypeScript, Golang, Rust | WEB3 fomo.moe

Full-stack Developer TypeScript, Golang, Rust | WEB3 fomo.moe

Full-stack Developer TypeScript, Golang, Rust | WEB3 fomo.moe

Slow Postgres, part 1 of 8. The SQL and raw numbers for every test are on GitHub.

You add an index on status, run EXPLAIN, and Postgres reads the whole table anyway. ANALYZE doesn't change the plan. Someone suggests SET enable_seqscan = off, the plan finally shows your index, and the query gets slower.

Usually the planner is right. It prices a plan by the 8 KB pages it has to read and by whether it reads them in order or jumps around between them, and once you count pages the same way, you can answer most "why is it ignoring my index" tickets yourself.

This series started as my notes from an open lesson on slow Postgres queries by balun.courses. The tests and numbers are my own.

One note before the numbers: the AlphaVPS link at the end is a referral link, so I may get a commission at no extra cost to you, and the netcup vouchers come from my own account.

A regular B-tree index keeps only keys, the values it is sorted by, and next to each key a TID: the row's address in the heap, which is the table's main storage.

A TID is a page number plus a slot on that page. You can see it as the hidden ctid column:

Row 1000 is slot 48 on page 7. An index lookup for 'chargeback' returns a list of addresses like these, and Postgres then visits each of those heap pages to fetch the row and check that your transaction can see it.

The second step is the one people forget. To fetch one row, Postgres has to read the whole 8 KB page it sits on.

The lab runs on PostgreSQL 17.11 in Docker with default settings. My numbers come from a 4-vCPU, 8 GB cloud VM, but any small VPS or a laptop will do.

136 rows fit on a page, so 30,000 rows take 221 pages. I picked 30,000 because ANALYZE samples 300 × default_statistics_target rows, which is 30,000 at the default. On this table it reads every row, so the statistics are exact and your plans should come out the same as mine.

Ask for the most common value and the index goes unused:

Cost has no unit you can convert to milliseconds. It only means something next to another plan's cost.

The value you filter on appears nowhere in that formula. Ask for 'chargeback' with the index paths switched off and the Seq Scan still costs 596. Only the index path's price moves with the value, so the planner is choosing between a fixed price and a sliding one.

For 'paid', every one of the 221 pages holds paid rows, so the index path would read the whole heap plus the index. Force it with enable_seqscan = off and you get a Bitmap Heap Scan at cost 872.

Selectivity is the share of rows that pass the filter. The usual rule of thumb goes: one row, use the index; 1%, usually; 20%, it depends; 70%, Seq Scan. Here is the same table counted by pages as well as by rows:

The rule of thumb says index failed, and Postgres agrees: Index Scan at cost 235 against 596. Run both with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), though, and the index path touches 209 buffers to the Seq Scan's 221, a saving of twelve page reads.

It still finished faster, 0.19 ms versus 0.93, because checking 270 rows is less CPU work than filtering 30,000. For 'chargeback', 30 rows on 30 pages, the index path needs 32 buffers instead of 221.

Two things decide how rows land on pages. Row width sets how many fit on one, and at 136 rows per page any value much more common than 1 in 136 ends up on nearly every page. Physical order is the other. I spread failed evenly on purpose. If your failed orders came from one bad deploy on one afternoon, they'd sit on a few neighbouring pages and the index would look great.

On 221 pages everything finishes in a couple of milliseconds, so for timings I built a bigger table: 5 million rows, 326 MB, about 120 rows per page.

A bucket column holds a random number from 0 to 999,999, so WHERE bucket < 10000 matches 1% of the rows. I loaded the same rows twice, once in random order and once sorted by bucket, and forced each plan with the enable_* settings at shares from 0.01% to 50%. shared_buffers was 2 GB, which kept the whole table in memory.

For scattered rows Postgres picked a bitmap scan, which collects all the TIDs first and then reads each heap page once, in page order. Up to 10% of the rows it beat the Seq Scan, 98 ms to 124. At 25% it lost, 174 against 139, and the planner still chose it. A plain Index Scan, one heap visit per row, lost from 5% on.

By 10% the scattered matches sit on every single page, and the bitmap scan still won. It reads all 41,667 pages but checks only the 499,000 rows the bitmap points to, while the Seq Scan checks all 5 million. With the table in RAM a page read costs next to nothing, and the time goes into checking rows.

For clustered rows the index won at every share I tried, even 50%: 123 ms against 142.

RAM is the friendly case. For the cold runs I restarted Postgres and dropped the OS page cache before every run, so every page came off the VM's disk.

The Seq Scan got about twice as slow, 250 to 350 ms at every share. The clustered index won everywhere again, 23 ms versus 263 at 5%.

The scattered bitmap scan took 748 ms at 0.5% of rows, to the Seq Scan's 349. At 1% it took 1.27 seconds against 255 ms, five times slower, and that's the plan Postgres picks.

The bitmap scan at 2% read more heap pages than at 1%, 37,939 versus 29,143, and still finished more than six times faster, 190 ms against 1,275. From 2% to 10% it beat the Seq Scan again.

The 2% run touched 91% of the pages, so it was close to one long sequential read. The 1% run touched 70%, with holes in between. My best guess is OS readahead, which prefetches reads that look sequential and gives up when they're full of gaps. I haven't confirmed it yet.

The planner has no way to see that difference. All it has is random_page_cost = 4, a single guess at how much a jump costs next to a sequential read, and it used the same guess for both runs.

A 200-row copy shows the other end of the scale, where the table is too small for any index to win.

Only 2 of the 200 rows match, but reading two pages and checking 200 rows costs just 2 + 2 + 0.5 = 4.50. Turn off enable_seqscan and the cheapest index plan costs 6.19, because its one index page alone is priced as a random read at random_page_cost = 4. If you check plans on a 200-row test fixture, this is the arithmetic you're looking at, and it tells you nothing about the same query on 30 million rows in production.

"We're on SSDs, set it to 1.1." Fair, and on this table that flips the plan to an Index Scan at cost 2.77. Both versions finish in 10 microseconds or less, so on a table this size it makes no difference.

The one place for enable_seqscan = off is a scratch session, where it shows you what the other plan would cost. It applies to every query in the session, so in app code it also overrides the plans that were right, like 596 against 872 for 'paid'.

If the queries you care about only ask for the rare values, say a failed-payments dashboard or a chargeback queue, index only those rows:

It holds 3,000 entries instead of 30,000 and takes 5 pages, where the full index takes 28. Paid orders, 90% of the inserts here, never touch it.

Postgres only uses it when it can prove your filter implies the index's WHERE, and a literal status = 'chargeback' does. With only the partial index in place, a prepared status = $1 under a generic plan falls back to a Seq Scan, because the planner can't prove anything about a value it hasn't seen. Generic plans get their own part later in the series.

Before adding an index, look at the column in pg_stats:

That's what the planner believes about status as of the last ANALYZE. If most of your queries filter on paid, at 0.9, they get a Seq Scan, and no extra index will change that.

A negative n_distinct means a fraction of the row count. On tables bigger than the 30,000-row sample these numbers are estimates; you can raise the sample with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS.

The same view has a correlation column, the planner's idea of physical order. On my 5-million-row tables it was 0.01 for the scattered copy and 1 for the clustered one, and that difference in physical order is what separates the scattered and clustered lines in both charts.

Before CREATE INDEX, run the pg_stats query, relpages and the rows-versus-pages count on your own table. If the value you care about sits on most of the pages and the table doesn't stay in memory, the index won't save you reads.

All the numbers above come from one 4-vCPU AMD EPYC cloud VM with 8 GB of RAM, so yours will differ. The SQL, the scripts, the raw output and the chart code are on GitHub. Run them on your own server, and if you get a different picture or think I got something wrong, open an issue or a PR.

My own projects run on netcup (VPS from €2.21 a month) and AlphaVPS (VPS from €2.54 a month). If you need a box for this, either works.

For netcup I have a few €5 vouchers for new customers. Each one works once, so take one and leave the rest for the next person:

Paste it into the "Redeem voucher" field at the bottom of the netcup cart. If they're all gone, message me on LinkedIn and I'll send you a new one.

Good luck with your plans. Part 2 is next: how to read Postgres EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

#9793. A renamed cookie and a logout button that did nothing

Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at bbal-blog.kairo-app.workers.dev

Every automated test passed. I had tests for the password hash, for the rate limit, for the form validation. None of them pressed Exit and then asked whether the session still worked.

The reviewer found it by reading the logout file next to the login file. The two files used different names for the same thing, and that difference is easy to see when you read both in one sitting and easy to miss when you wrote them in different weeks.

When I rename something that appears in several files, I search the whole project for the old name before I call the job finished. When a feature touches security, I also ask what a user does with it: log in, log out, log in again, and see if the old session still works.

#9792. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9791. GITEX GLOBAL 2026 Puts AI Security, Cyber Resilience and Post-Quantum Readiness in Focus

Keeping you up to date with all the best events in tech.

Keeping you up to date with all the best events in tech.

Keeping you up to date with all the best events in tech.

As artificial intelligence moves from experimentation into critical business and government infrastructure, cybersecurity is facing a new set of challenges. Autonomous AI agents, increasingly interconnected systems, and growing concerns around data sovereignty are changing how organizations approach digital security. These developments will take center stage at GITEX GLOBAL 2026, taking place December 7–11 in Dubai, UAE. With a dedicated cybersecurity showcase, GITEX is bringing together global cybersecurity companies, government institutions, technology leaders, and industry experts to explore the next generation of digital defense.

Explore GITEX GLOBAL 2026: Register here.

One of the key cybersecurity highlights of this year's event is GITEX Cyber Valley, which will focus on AI security, dual-use cyber technologies, and post-quantum readiness.

As organizations increasingly deploy AI agents capable of making decisions and executing tasks, questions around accountability, access control, and operational security are becoming more urgent.

The challenge is no longer limited to protecting networks and endpoints. Organizations must also secure the data, infrastructure, and autonomous systems that increasingly power their operations.

GITEX Cyber Valley will bring these conversations together through tailored business meetings and private briefings for global cybersecurity leaders, creating opportunities to examine how organizations can scale AI capabilities while protecting the systems and information they depend on.

GITEX GLOBAL 2026 will feature an extensive lineup of cybersecurity companies showcasing technologies and solutions across the security ecosystem.

Confirmed cybersecurity exhibitors include Acronis, AMIVIZ, Cohesity, Commvault, Forcepoint, Forescout, Kaspersky, ManageEngine, NETSCOUT, Netskope, NinjaOne, Proofpoint, SentinelOne / Sentinel Labs, and Trellix.

Their participation reflects the breadth of the cybersecurity landscape, spanning data protection, endpoint security, network defense, threat detection, and enterprise resilience.

The UAE Cybersecurity Council will also participate, alongside other government institutions and public-sector entities, highlighting the importance of collaboration between national cybersecurity strategies and private-sector innovation.

The growing adoption of AI is creating new opportunities for businesses, but it is also expanding the attack surface.

AI-powered applications, autonomous agents, cloud infrastructure, and connected systems introduce new security considerations. Organizations must account for how AI systems access information, interact with other applications, and operate within critical business environments. At the same time, the emergence of quantum computing is prompting organizations to consider the long-term resilience of their encryption and data protection strategies.

These developments make AI security and post-quantum readiness increasingly important areas of discussion for cybersecurity professionals, technology providers, and government decision-makers.

GITEX GLOBAL's wider focus on sovereign AI, frontier models, agentic AI, and sovereign security provides a broader context for these discussions, connecting cybersecurity with the infrastructure and technologies shaping the next phase of digital transformation.

#9788. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9786. Packaging Innovation for Good

Founder @ NowSourcing & Innovate Summit | Contributor @ Hackernoon | Advisor: Google Small Biz, SXSW

Founder @ NowSourcing & Innovate Summit | Contributor @ Hackernoon | Advisor: Google Small Biz, SXSW

Founder @ NowSourcing & Innovate Summit | Contributor @ Hackernoon | Advisor: Google Small Biz, SXSW

The European Union has declared an ultimatum against unsustainability: all consumer packaging placed on the EU market must be designed for recycling by 2030.  This mandate was announced by the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) and formally became law in all 27 EU member states on Aug. 12, 2026.  Since then, the mandate has placed restrictions on synthetic “forever chemicals” (PFAS) in food packaging as part of the “Design for Recycling” (DfR) framework, which will become the baseline by 2030.  It is significantly reshaping how companies design, import and sell products globally.

All packaged products must meet these regulatory changes, not just those manufactured in the EU.  Because many brands prefer to standardize packaging across different nations’ markets, it is probable that PPWR’s influence will reach well beyond Europe as brands change their designs to streamline operations.

Under PPWR, materials will be graded based on their recyclability performance rates through the DfR framework.  Grade A materials are __≥95% recyclable__and meet the highest circular life cycle standards.  Grade B materials are ≥80% recyclable and are still considered to be highly efficient.  Materials graded as C are ≥70% recyclable.  Any material rated below 70% is deemed unrecyclable and will be banned from all markets.

The new rules imply that paperboard is one of the best materials for long-term reuse, reducing and recycling because it combines a high recyclability rate and excellent compatibility with set content targets.  This paper-based material can be recycled 5-10 times into innovative packaging for consumer retailers and their customers.  After it is responsibly disposed of, the cycle starts again for this valuable material.  European waste systems reportedly recover 87% of paper and paperboard packaging for reuse.  This significantly outperforms plastic, which has just a 42% recovery rate.  Other fiber-based materials help companies adjust to the tightening restrictions and mandates on single-use plastic packaging while simultaneously supporting enduring goals made for resource efficiency and overall recyclability.

The first rising concern about single-use plastics began in the 2010s.  By 2022, the European Commission proposed PPWR to replace the outdated Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive (PPWD) of 1994.  By February 2025, PPWR went into full effect.  In the coming years, the development of secondary legislation will start.  By 2028, mandatory standardized labels will appear on consumer packaging and on all waste sorting receptacles. Later on in the early 2030s, all packaging in the EU, whether locally produced or imported, will officially meet DfR criteria.  Most plastic packaging and plastic parts will meet initial minimum recycled content requirements.  By the end of the decade, all packaging must meet even stricter criteria for recyclability to ensure an even more sustainable world.

The PPWR intends to set a binding packaging waste reduction target of 15% by 2040.  Brands that adapt to the DfR mandates from the start by adopting paperboard material and designing for a circular material lifecycle will be better prepared for decades to come.  Additionally, they will also gain an advantage in a competitive market where environmental sustainability is rapidly becoming the criterion.

Looking at the Future of Tech in Healthcare

#9779. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

#9777. How to deal with anxious-ambivalent attachment in a relationship

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Have you ever texted your partner only to spiral into oblivion waiting for them to respond? You wonder if they’re upset with you, if you did something wrong, or if they’re quietly pulling away. When their response finally comes through, you exhale the biggest sigh of relief. And then you start second-guessing why you were so worried in the first place.

If this sounds familiar, you may be dabbling in the world of ambivalent attachment, which is one of many attachment styles formed in adolescence and carried into adulthood.

Ambivalent attachment is a relationship pattern where you want to feel close to your partner but can’t always get there. It can show up as craving reassurance but doubting it, swinging between feeling connected to your partner and fearing they’ll leave, or analyzing small interactions for a hidden meaning that often isn’t there. While it may feel overwhelming, this attachment style isn’t a flaw in your personality, but rather a pattern shaped by early experiences in your life.

Let’s unpack what ambivalent attachment means, how to spot the signs in adulthood, and what to do if you (or your partner) lean toward this attachment style. Plus, we’ll dive into how to create steadier, more supportive relationships that feel good for all involved.

Anxious-ambivalent attachment—also called ambivalent attachment—is a relationship pattern where you crave reassurance yet struggle to feel settled once it’s given. It’s like wanting to lean on someone but worrying they might step away just as you do.

In adult relationships, ambivalent attachment may show up as feeling unsure about your partner’s commitment to you, cycling between connection and doubt, or getting caught in emotional highs and lows depending on how available your partner feels to you.

While it can feel overwhelming, this isn’t a flaw. It’s a protective strategy learned early in life that can be reshaped over time.

Ambivalent attachment often develops in childhood when caregiving is inconsistent. Basically, sometimes you were nurtured, and sometimes you weren’t. This unpredictability creates uncertainty in children, as they learn that comfort may arrive (but not reliably), so they cling tightly when it does appear. Over time, this wires the nervous system to stay on high alert for signs of loss or disconnection.

While it may seem easy to blame the caregivers involved, that’s not always the best answer or solution. Many people provide inconsistent care because of stress, lack of support, or their own attachment struggles. The good news is that even if this style formed early, it can shift in adulthood through consistent experiences of safety and connection.

Ambivalent attachment doesn’t always look dramatic from the outside. It often shows up in subtle, everyday ways that leave both partners feeling drained or confused. While everyone feels insecure at times, people with an ambivalent attachment style experience these patterns more intensely and more often.

1. Constant need for reassurance: You might ask for confirmation of your partner’s love or commitment regularly through words, texts, or gestures. The tricky part for people with an ambivalent attachment style is that reassurance often doesn’t stick. Even after hearing “I love you,” doubt can creep back quickly, fueling the cycle for reassurance again.

2. Fear of abandonment: Small shifts in a partner’s behavior—like if they take longer than usual to reply to a message or are quieter than usual—can trigger unnecessary worry. The fear isn’t just about being left by your partner, it’s about being forgotten or no longer valued. And for someone with this attachment style, those fears can be dire.

3. Hyper-attunement to signals: People with ambivalent attachment often read between the lines of every interaction, scanning tone, body language, or text punctuation for hidden meaning. A short text that simply says, “K,” might feel like rejection rather than just brevity.

4. Emotional highs and lows: Relationships can feel like a rollercoaster. You may feel ecstatic when things feel close and connected, then anxious when any distance appears. The intensity of these swings can feel overwhelming for both partners.

5. Difficulty trusting stability: Even when the relationship is going well, there’s a lingering sense that it could change at any moment. This makes it hard to relax into intimacy, because safety doesn’t feel fully reliable.

6. Feeling “too much” or “not enough”: Self-doubt often runs in the background, accompanied by persistent worrying that your needs are excessive or fearing that you’re somehow lacking. This inner tug-of-war can make it difficult to feel secure in how you show up in a relationship.

Working with ambivalent attachment is about finding steadier ground, both within yourself and your relationships. These strategies combine self-regulation, clearer communication, and practical agreements that build trust over time.

1. Recognize and name the pattern: The first step is simply noticing when old fears are coming up. Take time to put a name to the feeling, and remind yourself that it’s a learned response and not proof that something is wrong with you or your relationship. Taking a beat to give your feelings a name gives you the chance to pause before you react impulsively.

2. Soothe your body before your thoughts: Ambivalent attachment often activates the nervous system, which can make worries feel louder than they are. Simple grounding tools, such as intentional breathing, a mindful walk, or even running cold water over your wrists (which may help calm your nervous system) can bring your body back to baseline. Once you’re calmer, you’ll have more perspective on what’s really happening.

3. Ask directly instead of protesting: Protest behaviors (testing someone, withdrawing your affection, or sending a string of texts from the top of your mind) can backfire and push your partner away instead of bringing them closer. Practice naming your needs clearly instead. Try saying something like, “I’m feeling anxious right now and could use reassurance that we’re okay.” It might feel vulnerable to be so honest and open, but being direct usually leads to better connection.

4. Build a personal reassurance toolkit: Instead of depending only on your partner for reassurance, create a set of resources you can turn to yourself. This might include rereading kind messages, journaling, doing grounding exercises, or calling a supportive friend. Having options beyond your partner reduces the sense of desperation when anxiety spikes.

5. Practice small steps toward trust: Shifting attachment styles takes time, but small experiments help. Try waiting a little longer than you typically would before sending a check-in text, and see how that feels. You can also remind yourself of past experiences where closeness stood the test of time or survived a disagreement. Each successful moment builds evidence that security is possible, even if your old fears insist otherwise.

💙 Looking for tips to self-soothe? Try the Calming Anxiety guided practice on the Calm app.

6. Offer steady reassurance with boundaries: Consistency may help calm anxiety. Simple habits like a morning check-in or saying when you’ll call back create predictability. But it’s also important to pair reassurance with realistic boundaries. You might say, “I can’t text during work, but I’ll check in at lunch.”

7. Respond to the need, not just the words: Underneath protests or big reactions is usually a fear of being abandoned. Instead of focusing only on the tone or delivery of something your partner says, try reflecting the underlying need. You can say, “I hear that you’re worried I’m pulling away, but I want you to know I’m here.” This validation often matters more than a perfect solution.

8. Set clear repair practices: When tensions rise, agree in advance on how to pause and return to the conversation when you’re level-headed. Try saying, “If one of us feels overwhelmed, we’ll take a 20-minute break and come back at an agreed time.” Returning as promised helps rebuild trust, strengthens your relationship, and makes conflicts feel less threatening.

💙 Need a little more support? Check out the Kind Communication meditation on the Calm app.

9. Create shared routines for connection: Structure helps balance anxiety. A weekly check-in, an agreed-upon text during the workday, or even a daily hug ritual can anchor the relationship. These small but predictable moments reduce the need for constant reassurance.

Related read: How to use words of encouragement: 50 examples

10. Name the cycle and work as a team: Instead of blaming each other, talk about the pattern: “We tend to argue when I get quiet, and you seek more closeness. How can we catch it earlier?” Naming the cycle makes it something you face together, rather than a flaw in either partner.

💙 Learn how to take A Purposeful Pause with Jay Shetty on the Calm app.

Ambivalent attachment usually begins in early childhood. When a caregiver is sometimes warm and attentive but other times distracted, stressed, or unavailable, a child learns that love is unpredictable. This inconsistency creates anxiety about whether comfort will be there when it’s needed most.

Over time, the child develops strategies to cling tightly to connection, like seeking closeness while bracing for it to disappear. It’s not always about neglect. Often, caregivers themselves are overwhelmed or carrying their own attachment wounds. But the result is the same, and it’s that love is both essential and unreliable.

You may notice repeating patterns in your relationships, like craving reassurance but rarely feeling settled when you receive it. Small shifts in your partner’s tone, attention, or texting habits may trigger outsized worry about abandonment.

Overthinking, analyzing, or swinging between feeling deeply connected and then uncertain are also common. If these patterns show up across multiple relationships, that can be a strong sign of ambivalent attachment.

Attachment styles can change. While your early experiences lay the foundation, your attachment style can shift as you build new experiences of safety and stability. Supportive relationships, therapy, and personal work on self-regulation all help strengthen secure attachment.

The process is gradual and often happens through repeated moments of repair and reassurance. Over time, these experiences retrain your nervous system to trust that closeness can last.

Both ambivalent and avoidant attachment come from early inconsistencies in caregiving, but they lead to opposite coping strategies. People with ambivalent attachment often lean in, seeking closeness, reassurance, and connection. Sometimes, these manifest in ways that feel intense or overwhelming to their partner.

People with avoidant attachment tend to lean out. They value independence, minimize their needs, and withdraw when relationships feel too vulnerable. Ambivalent attachment is marked by fear of abandonment, while avoidant attachment is marked by discomfort with intimacy.

Yes, therapy can be effective. Working with an attachment-focused therapist gives you a consistent relationship where trust and stability are practiced week after week. Different forms of therapy like Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT), schema therapy, and cognitive-behavioral therapy can help you identify old patterns, calm the nervous system, and create new relational habits.

Over time, the therapy relationship itself often serves as a secure base, making it easier to bring those new ways of relating into your everyday life.

Patience and predictability are key. Your partner may need more reassurance than you thought, so offering it consistently and directly can ease their anxiety. For example, sending a quick “thinking of you” text before a long meeting or confirming plans in advance can make a big difference.

At the same time, it’s important to set boundaries around what you can realistically give. A helpful approach is to offer what you can with warmth, and state what you can’t with clarity. That way, your partner feels cared for without you becoming overextended.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#9771. Skip Salt And Pepper: Add A Packet Of This Seasoning To Ground Beef For Delicious Burgers

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Aside from the fact that burgers are endlessly customizable in terms of toppings, you can change up what you put into the beef as well. For example, if you wanted a touch of sweet heat, you could actually add hot honey into your ground beef mix. Or some people fold the ground meat over pieces of cheese, in what's known, at least in Minnesota, as a Juicy Lucy. However, if you wanted to keep the flavor profile roughly the same as a classic burger, just with more savoriness (and a hint of sweetness), you could incorporate a packet of onion soup mix, and you wouldn't even need any extra salt or pepper. There are plenty of brands available, but Lipton's is popular for a reason, and is widely available at stores like Walmart.

Onion soup mix will give your burgers more depth of flavor than just ground beef seasoned with salt and pepper because it tends to include ingredients that are full of umami; in some cases, that might be straight-up MSG, a much maligned flavor enhancer that was the target of Asian racism starting in the 1960s. But MSG is perfectly safe, and more than that, it upgrades pretty much everything it goes in, giving it a meatier, richer taste, which, when it comes to burgers, sounds like exactly something you'd want.

Also, classic onion soup mix is already quite heavy on the sodium, with salt typically ranking near the top of the ingredient list. You can forgo adding any more, which, if you often forget to season your burgers (it happens), means this is the right hack for you.

Using onion soup mix in your ground beef before you form it into burger patties is an easy and inexpensive way to get your next cheeseburger (and meatloaf, for that matter) to sing; it's also shelf-stable, so you can keep it in your pantry for a year or so and always have some on hand. However, you don't want to overdo it on the onion soup packets. A good ratio is a single packet per two pounds of beef, so if you're only mixing a pound, you'll want to sprinkle in only half of the mix. This should keep it so that onion isn't the only thing you taste when you bite into the burger, but there's still enough so that those rich umami flavors can permeate throughout. And no, you still won't need salt or pepper.

It can also help to add a bit of water or beef broth before you knead the onion soup mix through. Three to four tablespoons should do it if you're using two pounds of beef, and again, halve that amount if you're only cooking up one. The water "activates" the soup mix, hydrating the dry ingredients, which are powdered concentrates. This will keep the burger moist, rather than having the soup mix suck all the juiciness out of the meat. Just be sure to incorporate the water until it is no longer powdery and not much more; you don't want your burgers to fall apart in the skillet or on the grill.

#9769. 11 Classic Italian Dishes That Belong On Your Thanksgiving Table

Italian food is inherently celebratory. The cuisine embodies togetherness, featuring giant loaves of semolina bread, big salads, and overflowing family-style platters that snake their way around the table until there's a little bit of everything on everyone's plate. And while we didn't all necessarily grow up eating meatballs, gnocchi, and lasagna, these meals have slowly become a fundamental part of the American cooking canon. Italian food isn't necessarily easy to prepare, but its familiarity and simple elegance make the dishes feel accessible, even if they're difficult to master.

Italian food is also so well suited for the holiday table because of its adaptability. Regardless of your culinary background or self-identified food heritage, most classic Italian dishes can be reconfigured to fit any cuisine or occasion, including Thanksgiving. When you think about it, the two are a natural fit. Italian food is hearty, cozy, and comforting, with plenty of creamy carbohydrates and hearty main courses. The same goes for your typical Thanksgiving fare, allowing this list to feature recipe ideas that blend the two. Think pumpkin-stuffed ravioli, turkey lasagna, and risotto topped with roasted butternut squash. These interesting mashups will undoubtedly bring some extra excitement (and cheese) to your upcoming holiday menu.

A whole roast turkey is one of the most divisive holiday dishes. Done correctly, it's succulent, juicy, and full of bold poultry flavor; prepared improperly, you're left with pounds of bland, boring meat. But you don't need to cook a 10-pound bird to get turkey on the Thanksgiving table. These slow-cooker Italian turkey and zucchini meatballs use classic Italian cooking methods and ingredients to bring Thanksgiving flair to the holiday table. Meatballs are typically viewed as casual fare, but with the right cooking techniques and seasonings, they can be just as delicious as anything.

This recipe calls for a mixture of ground turkey meat and shredded zucchini. Why? The zucchini helps the meatballs retain moisture and adds some savory vegetal notes to the meat. These two ingredients are paired with a supporting cast of garlic, egg, breadcrumbs, and Pecorino Romano cheese to round out the flavor and give the meatballs a firmer texture. More importantly, the slow cooking keeps the meatballs submerged in a homemade tomato sauce, trapping moisture and keeping that notoriously dry turkey meat nice and luscious. This technique not only makes perfectly prepared meatballs, but also lets you tend to Grandma and Cousin Peter without worrying about something else overcooking.

This rich turkey tomato Bolognese is another creative way to add turkey to your Thanksgiving feast without cooking, carving, and roasting a massive piece of poultry. Bolognese is essentially a slow-simmered Italian sauce made with tomatoes and ground meat. As it cooks, the ingredients meld together, creating a thick, stew-like consistency that's greater than the sum of its parts. Although it is typically made with ground beef or pork, you can easily substitute turkey without losing any of the dish's heartiness or texture. The aromatics give it a sweet undertone, and the white wine helps deglaze the pan, capturing those brown bits of concentrated flavor.

But what sets this recipe apart is another ingredient synonymous with an authentic Bolognese yet largely omitted in jarred varieties: milk. Dairy may seem like a strange addition, but it gives the sauce a smooth, rich texture and helps tenderize the meat. Equally important to building your Bolognese sauce is pairing it with the correct pasta. Spaghetti is the most common but not the best option (at least according to Ina Garten). Instead, choose something flatter with more surface area, like tagliatelle or pappardelle. If you're feeling tubular, go with a shape with a wider diameter, like rigatoni, so the sauce can get trapped inside.

Sausage has rightfully earned its place on the Thanksgiving table, so much so that you can find it in everything from stuffing to cornbread casseroles to white gravy. But depending on which style you choose, the meat can easily overpower or oversalt a dish. When preparing this zucchini involtini, it's best to use an uncooked, Italian-style sausage. Unlike those popular, pre-cooked, vacuum-sealed chicken sausages, a quality Italian sausage comes raw and in a natural casing; otherwise, you can't sufficiently break up, brown, and mix the meat with other ingredients.

This appetizer requires some preparation, but the final result is well worth the effort. The most laborious task is slicing the zucchini into long, thin planks and piping them full of the sausage and ricotta filling. After you prepare the rolls, the rest of the dish comes together quickly. Just top each one with shredded cheese, and bake them together in a thin layer of sauce. The chew of the sausage paired with the sweet tomato sauce and creamy ricotta makes for an unforgettable appetizer that tastes just as impressive as it looks. If you don't want to make your tomato sauce from scratch, you can easily substitute your favorite jarred marinara.

Agnolotti started in the Piedmont region of northern Italy as a humble, pinched pasta that farmers would make to use up leftover bits of meat. Unlike ravioli, which are perfectly square, agnolotti are thin and rectangular, more like a standard bedroom pillow rather than a throw. This agnolotti di zucca is the perfect seasonal pasta, especially if you're in the mood to make fresh dough.

And while many Thanksgiving centerpieces feature a cornucopia of squash and gourds, this recipe actually includes them in the dish, specifically in the agnolotti filling, which is made with a mixture of ricotta cheese and roasted delicata squash. If you don't want to deal with chopping and de-seeding, a pumpkin purée will also work, but the flavor may fall short without those natural caramel notes you get from freshly roasted squash. The fresh pasta is an excellent foil, the dough chewy and toothsome as it cradles the delicate filling. After the agnolotti are stuffed and boiled, they're finished in a pan with butter and sage for a bite that's all things autumnal. Obviously, this dish isn't exactly light fare, so serve it in place of your more classic holiday carbohydrates.

Speaking of ravioli, you can't have a list of classic Italian dishes without mentioning this instantly recognizable stuffed pasta. Moving beyond squash, this homemade ravioli recipe focuses on the other orange gourd: pumpkin. But we're not talking about the canned stuff; this dish gets its unique flavor from freshly roasted sugar pumpkin. Does it require more prep work? Yes. You have to remove the seeds and stringy pulp, roast the pumpkin, and scoop out the flesh, but these extra steps add a bright earthiness you just can't recreate with canned pumpkin.

Unlike most pasta fillings, which are salty, savory, and creamy, this recipe goes in another direction, pairing pulverized almonds with ground nutmeg, ricotta cheese, and, of course, roasted pumpkin. The finished ravioli are coated in a traditional butter-sage sauce, furthering that autumn feel. Again, these require homemade dough, but it's fairly forgiving if you roll it out to the proper thickness — slightly less than 1 millimeter thick. Cut the dough in circles, and fold over the filling to make pretty little half moons, a nice, festive homage to the fall harvest.

The Thanksgiving table is usually covered with the classics: stuffing, cornbread, turkey, and sweet potato casserole. But this predictability can easily veer into monotony. Change is difficult, but it can be a good thing, especially for your palate. Reinventing your holiday menu isn't so much about eliminating as it is about balancing. Holiday food is notoriously rich and sweet; adding a dish that's salty, spicy, and earthy can help bring some relief.

These spicy sausage stuffed mushrooms deliver all of the above. A stuffed mushroom is a festive appetizer, but if you use super-sized portobellos, they quickly become worthy of a main course. The stuffing is a mixture of spicy sausage, breadcrumbs, egg, and grated cheese. If you want to sacrifice a mushroom (or stems), you can dice it up and add it in there too. Once the filling is sautéed, all you need to do is clean and stuff your mushrooms, then bake until everything is cooked through. Compared to making and filling your own fresh pasta dough, this appetizer is pretty easy to throw together. You can also prepare these ahead of time and just bake them off when ready. The sausage's pepperiness, the crunch of the breadcrumbs, and the mushrooms' earthy, umami notes make this a definite crowd-pleaser.

Risotto is cultural fusion at its finest, blending northern Italian cooking traditions with the culinary influence of Middle Eastern traders and travelers. It's a simple dish that requires only a modest collection of ingredients. But don't be fooled by its understated appearance — risotto takes a lot of skill and patience to execute successfully. If you've ever tasted a quality risotto, you'll know its texture is what makes it so elegant and luxurious. As the Arborio rice cooks, the grains release their natural starches, creating a smooth, velvety texture without any cream.

This butternut squash and sage risotto follows the same basic principles, but its flavor profile leans more toward seasonal fall ingredients and isn't quite what you would find at a classic Italian restaurant. The butternut squash is diced into cubes, tossed with honey and olive oil, roasted, and served on top of the finished dish. But more important than the garnish is the cooking of the risotto itself. The Arborio rice should be lightly sautéed with oil and aromatics until opaque before receiving its first ladle of broth. From there, you're going one cup at a time, waiting for the grains to absorb the broth or stock before adding the next round of liquid. The risotto is ready when it naturally spreads across the plate.

Turkey is the iconic Thanksgiving centerpiece, but what really gets the whole family gathered around the table is the variety of smooth and scoopable side dishes. Nobody is surprised by mashed potatoes, macaroni and cheese, and corn pudding, but if you want something with more Italian flair and a nuttier, toastier finish, consider adding polenta to your menu.

Polenta is essentially a cornmeal porridge that's mounted with butter. It's rich and filling and probably the reason Uncle Bob will fall asleep before dessert. This polenta pasticciata (also known as "messed up" polenta) is like a mix of scalloped potatoes and a cheesy casserole. To make the dish, you cook, cool, and refrigerate the polenta in a baking dish until set. You then slice the polenta into half-inch-thick slices and stack them like a lasagna, adding alternating layers of polenta and cheese. This recipe also uses a trifle of fromage, including Gruyère, Gorgonzola dolce (an Italian blue cheese), and rich, creamy mascarpone. Finally, you bake the whole thing until golden brown and bubbly. Be forewarned: You may never be able to go back to eating an ordinary casserole ever again.

You can skip the turkey; you can ixnay the green bean casserole; you can even pass on the sweet potatoes, but it's hard to call it a Thanksgiving feast without stuffing. I never understood why we relegate this savory bread pudding to just one day of the year, as it's easy to put together, uniquely herby, and a great way to salvage that stale loaf. Given these characteristics, you can take your stuffing in hundreds of directions. But since this article focuses on classic Italian dishes, we're sticking with that cadre of ingredients.

At first glance, this sausage and mushroom stuffing seems relatively ordinary; it doesn't use a scoop of gochujang or soak its bread in a dashi broth. But if you look closer, you'll see it's special in its simplicity. It all starts with the bread, which is a nice, tart sourdough. Next is the spicy, porky, and piquant Italian sausage. Finally, it's the broth. Sure, you can use chicken stock, but this recipe calls for pouring your vermouth-infused broth back into the pan with the cooked fennel, onion, and celery to infuse it with that deep, naturally sweet vegetable flavor. Right before baking, you quickly cook your mushrooms and add them to the bread mixture with a sprinkling of fresh herbs. No superfluous additions here; each ingredient has a place and a purpose, which is why this makes for such a terrific stuffing.

It's hard to pinpoint exactly when macaroni and cheese made its way to the Thanksgiving table, but this classic comfort food is now somewhat of a holiday fixture. And while it's hard to find fault with any bubbling crock of cheesy noodles, if you want to deviate from this French-inspired dish and go Italian, make this turkey and spinach gnocchi Alfredo bake.

Rarely does one recipe have it all, but this one comes pretty close. The ingredient list could almost be healthy — if you closed your eyes before pouring in the cup of heavy cream. But it's not all richness upon richness. The foundation of this dish is diced — not ground — turkey breast, gnocchi, spinach, and cheese. Still, you'll find it surprisingly balanced, thanks to the turkey's meatiness and slightly gamey flavor. The sauce is made with turkey or chicken stock thickened with roux and finished with cream. After dousing the gnocchi in the sauce, topping with mozzarella, and baking in the oven, you'll have a show-stopping side dish that will likely upstage anything else on the table.

No matter the occasion — dinner party, sweet 16 celebration, competitive evening of Catan — a baking dish filled to the brim with bubbling waves of saucy pasta sheets and melted cheese always turns heads. Lasagna is that dish, always here to nourish and satisfy. A big tray can feed an army (of at least six) comfortably, all without the effort of preparing individual burgers, cutlets, steaks, or filets.

Traditional lasagna, or at least the one most of us know today, is an import from Southern Italian immigrants, made primarily with a simple meat ragu, ricotta cheese, and mozzarella (and pasta sheets, of course). This spinach turkey lasagna isn't much different, the main change being substituting ground turkey for ground beef. The ground turkey adds some extra chew and texture to the somewhat mushy lasagna. Using a leaner meat also helps cut down on the dish's overall richness and allows other flavors, like the spinach and marinara sauce, to shine. But most importantly, it's the fact that it's turkey that makes this minimal-fuss main course such a cool and tasty culinary crossover.

#9765. Giada De Laurentiis Has 3 Tips For Buying The Highest Quality Pasta At The Grocery Store

Every good pasta dish needs to be accompanied by a beautifully made sauce, but before the sauce, the cheese, and the garnish, there's the dried pasta itself. Of course, choosing the right shape counts, but that's only half the story. See, not all pasta brands are created equal. The next time you're walking down the pasta aisle, don't just pick one at random and hope for the best. Instead, borrow these three tips from Food Network legend Giada De Laurentiis to guarantee only the highest quality pasta ends up in your grocery cart. According to De Laurentiis, the pasta only needs water and durum wheat semolina, and it should be bronze-cut or slow-dried and have a rough texture.

De Laurentiis' tips are simple, as they are effective. When putting them all next to each other, the ingredients tip is arguably the most important by a significant margin. Semolina is a coarse, hard wheat flour with high protein and gluten levels, helping the pasta hold its shape and maintain its al dente bite. It should go without saying that dried pasta only needs water and durum wheat. No more, no less. In fact, for Italians, this doesn't represent high quality, but rather the baseline. Over there, the law mandates that any commercially sold "dried pasta" must be made strictly from 100% durum wheat semolina and water.

Unfortunately, the same rule doesn't apply here in the U.S., so some dried pastas are, for lack of better words, "enriched" with additives, preservatives, and certain brands, to the horror of Italians everywhere, even drop the semolina (which just refers to the coarse grind) in favor of finer-ground durum wheat flour, which just can't match the texture of semolina. If you spot any extra add-ins or swaps on the ingredient list, it's a telling sign that brand belongs nowhere near your plate.

We're putting Giada de Laurentiis' first tip ahead of the other two for a reason. If a box doesn't list just semolina durum wheat and water, chances are it won't pass these other checks either. Her second and third tips involve looking at the packaging. For high-quality pasta that goes above and beyond, look for "bronze cut" and "slow dried" on the box or bag.

Traditional artisan makers dry pasta slowly at low temperatures, and the most patient can take as long as six days. Mass-market brands don't have time to be sitting around, and so they blast the pasta with high heat and have it dry in a matter of hours — you can tell this was the case when the pasta is bright yellow rather than a pale, ivory white. This is about more than just cutting corners. Makers argue that low temperatures preserve the wheat's natural flavor and protect the gluten structure, which helps the pasta cook evenly and keep its bite.

Bronze cut refers to how the pasta is extruded (pushed through a die to be shaped), and it leads right into De Laurentiis' third tip. Traditional makers use dies made of bronze, which leave the pasta's surface rough, matte, and slightly powdery. Most mass-produced pasta is pushed through smooth, Teflon-coated dies instead, which leave it smooth and shiny. To some, this might be more aesthetically pleasing, but that stops mattering once the sauce enters the picture. Pasta's job is to carry the sauce, and the coarse surface of bronze-cut gives it more to cling to, while smooth pasta doesn't have a textured surface for the sauce to grip. Even if the label doesn't say bronze-cut, you can usually tell just by looking whether it has texture or not.
